The entire supplied transcript, 0:00 to 9:10, was read. The closing fragments are incomplete. No source URL, speaker identity, local images or video embed are supplied. No unseen boards or missing speech were reconstructed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Preserved evidence\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Exact Markdown clip](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/LSAT%20Demon%20%20Abstract%20Conditionals.md), 6,712 bytes.\\r\\n- [Provenance](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/PROVENANCE.md) and [hash manifest](../../raw/sources/clips/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals-2026-10-03/SHA256SUMS).\\r\\n- SHA-256: `89a4f5266dc577f09ea99de2a21b77c10d7887724d140e823a04c89b9e1129ee`.\\r\\n- Publication and capture dates unknown. Inbox last-write date was 2026-10-03. Archived and ingested 2026-10-03. Original retained unchanged; no matching archived hash or completed source summary found before intake.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What the transcript actually contains\\r\\n\\r\\n| Timestamp | Source content, paraphrased | Scope and use |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 0:44–1:37 | Boston implies Massachusetts. Not being in Boston does not settle whether a person is in Massachusetts. Not being in Massachusetts excludes Boston. | Compare absent sufficient with absent necessary. Use an original familiar relationship. |\\r\\n| 1:37–3:04 | A stipulated psychology/sociology rule can be accepted for the question even if real course registration works differently. The speaker offers several equivalent forms. | Teach students to reason from the supplied rule, without inventing an explanation for why it exists. |\\r\\n| 3:27–3:56 | Swap the conditions and negate both to form the contrapositive. | Reserve the symbolic operation until the concept and notation have been taught. |\\r\\n| 4:19–5:34 | Progress to X → ¬Y and its contrapositive Y → ¬X; paraphrase using only if and unless. | Negative conditions and abstract labels belong after the notation prerequisites. Unless stays in its later language lesson. |\\r\\n| 6:06–7:36 | Critique unsupported conclusions from ¬Y, then use a smoking/health analogy to make the reverse error concrete. | Keep the counterexample technique; replace the medical example and check both proposed conclusions. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are narrated prompts and demonstrations, not a formal supplied question set. The clip names student concerns about abstract rules. It does not provide a bank of standalone questions, choices or a reviewed answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## An explicit transcript discrepancy\\r\\n\\r\\nAt 6:06 the transcript criticizes deriving **¬X** from **¬Y** under **X → ¬Y**. At 6:34 it criticizes deriving **X** from **¬Y**. These are different proposed conclusions. Both are unsupported, but the transcript shifts between them. We cannot identify whether this was a speaker correction or transcription error without playback.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe logically correct teaching point is: given X → ¬Y and ¬Y, X could be true or false. Both X/¬Y and ¬X/¬Y satisfy the rule. Preserve the discrepancy as evidence; do not silently attribute a polished, consistent exercise to the source.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original adaptations for the bootcamp\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the [existing source map](../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) and [selected voice](../../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md). These are newly authored examples inspired by the teaching functions above, not source quotations or published assignments.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Familiar inclusion:** Every square is a rectangle. A shape is not a square. Can it still be a rectangle? Yes. A rectangle with unequal adjacent sides supplies a possible case. Use only if these shape meanings are clear; the logic must not turn into a geometry test.\\r\\n2. **Stipulated rule:** Every ticket in Drawer R has a blue border. A ticket is in Drawer R. What follows? It has a blue border. The exercise does not need to explain why tickets were sorted this way.\\r\\n3. **Wording comparison:** “Only blue-bordered tickets are in Drawer R” and “A ticket is in Drawer R only if it has a blue border” both express Drawer R → Blue border. Ask learners to choose the matching relationship and explain what the sentence requires.\\r\\n4. **Negative-condition transfer:** If a room is showing a film, it is not hosting a workshop. The room is not hosting a workshop. Does that settle whether a film is showing? No. Ask the learner to build two possible rooms: film/no workshop and no film/no workshop. Both fit. This directly demonstrates why the reverse inference fails.\\r\\n5. **Delayed abstract retrieval:** After the negative-condition lesson, show X → ¬Y and ask which fact rules out X. Y does, because X would require ¬Y. Ask separately what ¬Y establishes about X: nothing definite. Keep the two questions distinct.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Do not import these source habits\\r\\n\\r\\n- Saying a rule no longer matters when one trigger is absent. Keep it available for later facts and other inferences.\\r\\n- Profanity, ridicule or dismissive characterizations of a learner\'s reasoning.\\r\\n- Smoking as a universally sufficient condition for an undefined “not healthy.” That analogy introduces vague and contestable content unrelated to learning the inference.\\r\\n- Legacy Logic Games framing, source promotion or unsupported learning guarantees.\\r\\n- The source\'s hurried “the only”/“must” sentence as a clean indicator template. Use a grammatical original and preserve obligation versus compliance.\\r\\n- Unless/without before their transformations have been taught. Keep all topic prerequisites in the existing 13-part progression and later-unit boundaries.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [sufficient/necessary clip](lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary.md), [LSAT Lab supplement](lsat-lab-conditional-logic-clip.md), [selected voice source](conditional-reasoning-voice.md).\\r\\n"}}}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 10.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 12877)\nTotal output lines: 3\n\n{"i":0,"r":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"4b1859","wall_time_seconds":1.1349012,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":14207,"output":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 14207)\\nTotal output lines: 628\\n\\n---\\r\\ntype: synthesis\\r\\nsubject: LSAT teaching voice standard\\r\\ncreated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-03\\r\\naliases: [LSAT voice reference, Conditional transcription writing standard]\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, writing]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# LSAT teaching: make the reasoning sound like someone thinking\\r\\n\\r\\n**This is Joshua\'s selected reference for writing LSAT teaching material.** Use it for bootcamp lessons, lecture notes, explanations, guided examples, drills, flashcards, quizzes, reference pages, and instructional feedback. It develops the teaching-content register in [the canonical teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md). That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. The goal is to reproduce those qualities closely through original wording and examples. The central quality is patient, conversational reasoning that the reader can follow and eventually perform.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is a calibration example. This guide separates **observed features** from **instructions for our material**. A source habit is not automatically a rule, a research finding, or permission to import a topic. Matching the voice does not require repeating the same metaphors, anecdotes, exercise sentences, or personal claims.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the part you need\\r\\n\\r\\n- [The evidence and coverage](#the-evidence-and-coverage)\\r\\n- [The voice in one original passage](#the-voice-in-one-original-passage)\\r\\n- [How the teacher relates to the reader](#how-the-teacher-relates-to-the-reader)\\r\\n- [Sentence length and spoken cadence](#sentence-length-and-spoken-cadence)\\r\\n- [Word choice and useful verbal habits](#word-choice-and-useful-verbal-habits)\\r\\n- [Questions that make the reader think](#questions-that-make-the-reader-think)\\r\\n- [Transitions, repetition, metaphor, and emphasis](#transitions-explain-why-the-next-move-follows)\\r\\n- [The complete source progression and depth](#the-complete-source-progression-and-depth)\\r\\n- [What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp](#what-to-carry-into-the-conditional-bootcamp)\\r\\n- [Accuracy and method boundaries](#accuracy-and-method-boundaries)\\r\\n- [Calibration examples and review](#calibration-examples-for-different-lsat-surfaces)\\r\\n- [A reusable writing brief](#a-reusable-writing-brief)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The evidence and coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [source summary](../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) identifies the [preserved HTML](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html), [provenance](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/PROVENANCE.md), and SHA-256. Every supplied section, FAQ entry, table, worked diagram, and drill item was read. HTML line references below refer to that unchanged archived file.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe document has six main sections and six subordinate headings. It ends with six basic drill items and an answer-key reference. One line is explicitly marked partially obscured. The answer key is not supplied. This analysis covers the entire attachment; it cannot reconstruct the missing line or establish the contents of the larger chapter.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML says its formatting was adjusted. We can examine what a pause, table, side note, or separated example does for learning. We cannot claim its font, spacing, color, or CSS exactly reproduces the original publication. No author is identified in the file. The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. The sentence makes the same guarantee for anyone enrolled in law school: they\'re a student.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Could someone be enrolled in law school without being a student? No. That would be an exception to a sentence that allows no exceptions. So being enrolled in law school doesn\'t just make being a student likely. ## assistant

Use this definition **before** the existing law-school example:

> **Sufficient means enough.** A sufficient condition gives you enough information to know that another condition is true. Once you know the sufficient condition is true, the other condition must be true too. You don't need another fact to establish it.
>
> That's what **guarantee** means here: the sufficient condition cannot be true while the other condition is false.

Then retain:

> If you're enrolled in law school, you're a student.
>
> Knowing you're enrolled in law school is enough to know you're a student. You don't need to know which law school you attend or which classes you're taking.

Replace the cause aside with:

> **Enough does not mean the only way**
>
> Being enrolled in law school is enough to know you're a student. That doesn't make law-school enrollment the only way to be a student.
>
> If you aren't enrolled in law school, you could still be a student. Not meeting a sufficient condition does not, by itself, rule out the other condition.

This teaches three distinctions: **enough information → certainty → other possibilities remain open**. It avoids making the definition depend on wording or introducing a separate causality topic.

Source support:

- [LSAT Lab transcript, 00:33–01:04](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt:52): sufficient condition true requires the other condition true. At 01:14–01:43, an absent sufficient condition leaves the other unsettled.
- [Demon sufficient/necessary, 01:48–02:15](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-sufficient-necessary.md:29): sufficient means enough.
- [Demon mastering conditionals](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-mastering-conditional-statements.md:28): a sufficient route need not be the only route.
- [Demon abstract conditionals, 00:44–01:37](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/sources/lsat-demon-abstract-conditionals.md:27): absence of the sufficient condition leaves both possibilities open.
- [Joshua’s corrections](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md:31): explain guarantee and sufficient in ordinary language before relying on them.

No edits made.
